title: How to Improve School Cultures, Part 2: Collins' Level 5 Leadership
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Part 2 of a series on improving school culture, this post applies Jim Collins' Level 5 leadership from Good to Great to schools. Stuart warns that knowing the concept is not enough; teachers and superintendents alike must pursue it relentlessly rather than impair culture through blame-shifting and credit-taking. He compiles Collins' descriptions of Level 5 leaders as humble and ferocious, ambitious for the institution rather than themselves, and quick to look in the mirror for failure and out the window for success. He cautions against reading Level 5 as mere servant leadership by stressing Collins' point about stoic resolve and intolerance of mediocrity. He adds that Level 5 leaders tend to come from inside the organization, and closes with a disclaimer that schools are not businesses but that he reads widely. Much of the body is quoted from Collins, so Stuart's own contribution is the application and framing.
points: Stuart frames Level 5 leadership as a path to better school culture that applies to anyone from classroom teacher to superintendent.
He pairs Collins' humility with his ferocious resolve, urging readers not to miss the tiger in the Level 5 description.
The window and mirror analogy gives a practical self-check: credit others for success, own failure.
Collins' finding that most good-to-great CEOs came from inside the company is used to argue that Level 5 leaders can be found among existing staff.
A disclaimer clarifies that borrowing from business does not mean schools and companies need identical skills.
quotes: Woe to us when we can cite Collins' Good to Great even as we habitually impair school cultures through things like blame-shifting, credit-taking, and self-promotion.

In short, Level 5 leaders are the kind of people who look outside the “window” when things go well — they attribute success to external factors — and look in the “mirror” when things don't go well — they take responsibility for failure.
I find so much to be refreshed by here. I don't need to be larger than life to create a better culture in my classroom or school.

But humility is only half of what Collins and his team observed in the good-to-great companies. He writes, “It's equally about ferocious resolve, an almost stoic determination to do whatever needs to be done to make the company great.
What could school cultures be like with a bunch of humble tigers running around? Answer: awesome.
It doesn't take some epic search to find your next Level 5 PLC leader or principal or superintendent or to find the Level 5 leader in yourself.
So: if you want to improve your school culture (and we all need to because cultures are like gardens that need constant tending), Level 5 leadership offers good food for thought.
